summary: This standards-track document describes RADIUS, a protocol that carries authentication, authorization and configuration information between a network access server and a shared authentication server. It was replaced by RFC 2865.

eli5.summary: The front desk checks a central guest list to see who may enter and what they can do.

questions: what is a nas in radius
subtitle: A protocol for a network device to verify that a user is authorized and to learn what service to give them.

tldr.problem: Network access servers (like dial-in servers) need to verify users' identities and determine what services they are allowed to use, but storing user databases on each server is impractical and insecure.
tldr.mechanism: RADIUS implements a client-server model where the network access server (client) sends authentication requests to a central RADIUS server with the username, password (encrypted), and details of the connection attempt. The server checks the user and returns an accept, reject, or challenge response, optionally including configuration parameters for the connection.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can maintain a single user database for authentication and authorization across many devices. It was replaced by RFC 2865, which is the modern RADIUS standard.

today: RFC 2138 was obsoleted by RFC 2865, the current standard for RADIUS, published in June 2000 with clarifications and additions. RADIUS remains widely used for dial-in and WiFi authentication.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) manages authentication, authorization, and configuration for network access. It operates as a client-server protocol where a Network Access Server (NAS)—such as a dial-in server or wireless access point—acts as a client and a centralized RADIUS server authenticates users and returns configuration parameters.

Key features include: a client-server model where the NAS passes user credentials to the RADIUS server and acts on the response; network security through shared secrets and encrypted passwords, preventing plaintext transmission on untrusted networks; support for multiple authentication methods (PPP PAP, CHAP, Unix login); and an extensible protocol using variable-length attribute-value tuples, allowing new attributes to be added without disrupting existing implementations.
sections.eli5: A dial-in server (NAS) asks a RADIUS server about a user instead of checking a local database. The server replies with 'approved' or 'rejected' and can send settings like IP address or time limits for the connection.

sections.title: Basic Operation
sections.content:
When a user connects to an NAS and provides credentials, the NAS creates an Access-Request packet containing the username and encrypted password, plus identifiers like the NAS IP address and port number. The packet is sent to the RADIUS server via UDP on port 1812 (or historically 1645).

The RADIUS server validates the sending NAS by checking for a shared secret configured for that client. If the NAS is unknown or the request is invalid, the server silently discards the packet. Otherwise, it looks up the user and verifies the password. The server may also check restrictions (like which ports or NAS devices the user can access) and may query other authentication systems.

The server responds with one of four packet types: Access-Accept grants access and includes configuration parameters (IP address, MTU, compression, timeouts, etc.); Access-Reject denies access with an optional text message; Access-Challenge requests further authentication (for challenge-response authentication schemes); or in rare cases, the server sends no response (timeout), prompting the NAS to retry or try an alternate server.

For challenge-response, the server sends an Access-Challenge with a text message and optional State attribute. The user responds, the NAS sends a new Access-Request with the response encrypted, and the State attribute from the challenge. The server validates and either grants access or sends another challenge.
sections.eli5: A user logs in, the NAS asks the RADIUS server 'Is this person OK?'. The server checks and says yes or no. If it's a challenge (like a code from a hardware token), the NAS asks again with the user's response, and the server confirms.

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
Every RADIUS packet starts with a fixed header of 20 octets. The Code field (1 octet) identifies the packet type (1=Access-Request, 2=Access-Accept, 3=Access-Reject, 11=Access-Challenge). The Identifier field (1 octet) helps match requests and replies. The Length field (2 octets) specifies the total packet length (minimum 20, maximum 4096).

The Authenticator field (16 octets) serves two purposes: in Access-Request packets, it is a random Request Authenticator generated by the NAS; in reply packets, it is a response authenticator calculated using MD5 over the reply code, ID, length, Request Authenticator, and reply attributes, using the shared secret as a key. This design lets the NAS verify that replies truly come from the server.

Following the header, the packet contains zero or more attributes, each with a type (1 octet), length (1 octet) including the type and length fields, and value (variable). Common attributes include User-Name, User-Password, NAS-IP-Address, NAS-Port, Service-Type, Framed-Protocol, Framed-IP-Address, Framed-IP-Netmask, Reply-Message, and Vendor-Specific. The User-Password attribute is encrypted using an MD5-based cipher with the shared secret.
sections.eli5: A RADIUS packet is like an envelope with a header saying what kind of message it is (question or answer), who sent it, how long it is, and a signature. Then there's a list of details: username, encrypted password, which port they're on, what service they want, etc.

sections.title: Authentication Methods
sections.content:
RADIUS supports multiple authentication mechanisms. For PAP (Password Authentication Protocol), the NAS includes the username and password directly in the Access-Request as User-Name and User-Password attributes (encrypted), optionally with Service-Type=Framed-User and Framed-Protocol=PPP.

For CHAP (Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol), the NAS generates a random challenge (ideally 16 octets), sends it to the user, and receives back a CHAP response with a CHAP ID. The NAS then sends an Access-Request with the username as User-Name and the CHAP response as a CHAP-Password attribute. The challenge can be placed in a CHAP-Challenge attribute or in the Request Authenticator if it is exactly 16 octets.

The RADIUS server validates CHAP by retrieving the user's password in cleartext, encrypting the challenge using MD5 with the CHAP ID and password, and comparing to the received CHAP-Password. If passwords are not available in cleartext (e.g., hashed storage), the server must return Access-Reject.

RADIUS also supports challenge-response authentication with hardware tokens or software generators. The server sends an Access-Challenge with a text message describing the challenge, and the NAS displays it to the user. After the user provides the response, the NAS sends a new Access-Request with the response as the User-Password, preserving the State attribute from the challenge.
sections.eli5: Different authentication methods work differently. PAP is simplest: send the password. CHAP is safer: the user encrypts a number the server gives them. Token authentication is most secure: the user has a device or app that generates a unique code for each login.

sections.title: Design Rationale and Attributes
sections.content:
RADIUS uses UDP instead of TCP for several technical reasons. First, RADIUS is transaction-based and must support failover to alternate servers, so retransmission timers are needed at the application layer anyway. Second, RADIUS does not require TCP's aggressive retransmission or acknowledgement overhead; users are willing to wait several seconds for authentication but not several minutes. Third, RADIUS's stateless nature (each client and server opens UDP once and reuses it through network failures) eliminates TCP's connection state issues. Fourth, UDP simplifies server implementation, allowing single-threaded servers to spawn separate processes for each request without managing TCP connections.

RADIUS defines numerous attributes to carry authentication, authorization and configuration information. Examples include User-Name (1), User-Password (2), NAS-IP-Address (4), NAS-Port (5), Service-Type (6), Framed-Protocol (7, like PPP or SLIP), Framed-IP-Address (8), Framed-IP-Netmask (9), Framed-Routing (10), Filter-Id (11), Framed-MTU (12), Framed-Compression (13), Login-IP-Host (14), Login-Service (15), Reply-Message (18), State (24), Class (25), Vendor-Specific (26), Session-Timeout (27), Idle-Timeout (28), and many others. New attributes can be registered with IANA without changing the protocol structure.
sections.eli5: RADIUS chose UDP because it did not need TCP's complexity or slow recovery from server failures. It needed to support fast switching to backup servers and did not require guaranteed in-order delivery. The protocol also uses a list of named attributes (like 'Service-Type' or 'Session-Timeout') so new features can be added without breaking old servers.

fields.desc: Packet type (1 for Access-Request, 2 for Access-Accept, 3 for Access-Reject, 11 for Access-Challenge)

fields.name: Authenticator
fields.desc: 16-octet random value (request) or MD5-based response validation code
